data.abstract:
O artigo apresenta uma experiência formativa que deu origem ao projeto de pesquisa em andamento, aprovado pelo Comitê de Ética em Pesquisa (CEP), no âmbito do Programa de Pós-graduação em Ensino, vinculado à linha de pesquisa Ensino de Linguagens e seus Códigos da Universidade de Cuiabá. Trata-se de uma experiência sobre o uso da Inteligência Artificial (IA), com foco no ChatGPT, no contexto da Educação Superior. A atividade ocorreu em formato de minicurso, realizado durante a Semana Acadêmica da instituição, reunindo docentes de diferentes áreas do conhecimento. O objetivo foi explorar as potencialidades pedagógicas da IA e estimular reflexões sobre seus impactos éticos, sociais e educacionais. A metodologia adotada baseou-se na observação participante, que possibilitou acompanhar de forma próxima as interações e significados atribuídos pelos professores. Os resultados evidenciaram benefícios, como a agilidade na produção de materiais didáticos e a personalização de planos de aula e os desafios relacionados às desigualdades no letramento digital, às condições institucionais de acesso e às preocupações éticas sobre autoria e papel docente. Conclui-se que a integração crítica da IA demanda processos permanentes de formação docente, capazes de articular inovação tecnológica, intencionalidade pedagógica e compromisso social.
Palavras-chave: Tecnologias Digitais. Cultura Digital. Observação Participante. Formação Docente. Prática Pedagógica Inovadora.
Abstract
This article presents a formative experience that originated the ongoing research project approved by the Research Ethics Committee (CEP), within the Graduate Program in Teaching, linked to the Research Line Teaching of Languages and their Codes at the University of Cuiabá. It reports an experience on the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI), focusing on ChatGPT, in the context of Higher Education. The activity took place in the form of a short course conducted during the institution’s Academic Week, gathering professors from different fields of knowledge. The aim was to explore the pedagogical potential of AI and to foster reflections on its ethical, social, and educational impacts. The adopted methodology was based on participant observation, which made it possible to closely follow the interactions and meanings attributed by the professors. The results revealed benefits such as agility in producing teaching materials and the personalization of lesson plans, as well as challenges related to inequalities in digital literacy, institutional access conditions, and ethical concerns about authorship and the teacher’s role. It is concluded that the critical integration of AI requires continuous teacher education processes capable of articulating technological innovation, pedagogical intentionality, and social commitment.
Keywords: Digital Technologies. Digital Culture. Participant Observation. Teacher Education. Innovative Pedagogical Practice.

data.abstract: With the rapid rise of large language models like ChatGPT, generative AI (GenAI) is transforming language education. This study investigates prompt engineering in a college English writing course, showing how structured prompts scaffold the writing process. By aligning prompt types with stages of academic writing, the framework systematizes GenAI use and extends theories of scaffolding and meta-cognition. data.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in engineering education, offering rapid content generation, intelligent code assistance, and simulation support. In Digital Electronics courses, AI can accelerate circuit design workflows, enhance self-regulated learning (SRL), and support deeper engagement with domain-specific concepts. This paper presents an engineering-adapted Human-Centered Learning and Teaching Framework (HCLTF) that integrates generative AI into the learning process while preserving analytical rigor and human-centered pedagogical values. The framework aligns with SRL's forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases, embedding AI in logic design, HDL development, simulation, and optimization tasks. A case study is presented in which 187 undergraduate students across three institutions design, simulate, and optimize a 4-bit synchronous up/down counter using a combination of traditional design methods and AI-assisted support. The AI was employed for Boolean simplification verification, Verilog code scaffolding, testbench generation, and timing optimization. AI-assisted workflows reduce HDL development time by 40% compared to traditional methods. Synthesis results reveal measurable differences between manual and AI-generated designs, including a 4.2% lower Fmax, 20% higher LUT usage, and a 9.5% increase in dynamic power prior to student-led optimization. Quantitative and qualitative findings indicate improvements in students’ Boolean reasoning, debugging proficiency, and reflective judgment across SRL phases. The study highlights the pedagogical value of guided GenAI integration and provides a scalable model for embedding AI-supported learning within Digital Electronics and broader engineering curricula.

data.abstract: Emergence of generative AI has created new possibilities for academic writing support. However, there are concerns that students may become overly reliant on AI-generated content and less involved in the writing process. This paper developed and evaluated Beementor, an AI chatbot grounded in self-regulated learning (SRL) to support students' academic essay writing across goal setting, planning, drafting, monitoring, feedback, and reflection. The chatbot was developed using the Successive Approximation Model (SAM), which consists of preparation, iterative design, and iterative development. An embedded mixed-method evaluation was conducted to explore students' user experience, academic writing performance, and the relationship between initial SRL and writing outcomes. The pilot implementation included expert reviewers, small-group users, and 62 undergraduate students. UX data indicated a positive perception of Beementor among students, with high scores for Cognitive Helpfulness, Emotional Support/Companionship, Interaction Quality, and Motivation and Engagement. The overall UX score was high $(\mathrm{M}=3.90, \text{SD} = 1.07)$, with Emotional Support/Companionship scoring the highest. The students' academic writing performance was observed to improve from pretest $(\mathrm{M}=37.26, \text{SD}= 16.11)$ to post-test $(\mathrm{M}=77.57, \mathrm{SD}=21.16)$, with a large effect size. However, there was no significant association between initial SRL and post-test writing scores or writing gain. The findings indicate that Beementor has the potential to be an SRL-based writing companion for academic writing processes and outcomes, but further research is needed with control groups and fully matched datasets.

data.abstract: Abstract This research examines how the use of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) influences university student creativity in collaborative learning environments that employ design thinking methodologies. Drawing on constructivist learning theory and creativity research, we conducted five classroom experiments in which student groups completed assignments. In four of these experiments, involving assignments scaffolded by design thinking, groups that used GAI tools consistently produced solutions evaluated as less creative than those generated without the help of GAI. In a fifth, non-design thinking assignment included for comparison, this pattern was not observed. These findings suggest that while GAI may assist with aspects of the design thinking process, its use can undermine creative engagement when it replaces rather than supports human ideation and reflection. Our results challenge assumptions about the benefits of GAI for creativity, particularly in collaborative university settings where design thinking is employed.

data.abstract:
Purpose of the article The article examines the evolution of artificial intelligence in higher education, tracing the progression from early intelligent tutoring systems and pedagogical conversational agents to contemporary large language model–based digital tutors. Its purpose is to synthesise current evidence on how these technologies influence learning processes, academic performance and institutional practices, and to assess the pedagogical opportunities and risks associated with their integration.
Methodology/methods The paper adopts a narrative systematic review design. Peer-reviewed sources, including meta-analyses, systematic reviews, umbrella reviews and domain-specific empirical syntheses published between 2011 and 2025 were analysed. Data extraction focused on research aims, methodological features, AI system types, educational contexts and reported outcomes. A thematic synthesis approach was used to identify recurring patterns and to develop an integrative conceptual framework describing the transition from chatbots to digital tutors.
Scientific aim The scientific aim is to provide a comprehensive and conceptually coherent account of the pedagogical functions, limitations and transformative potential of AI-enabled tutoring systems, and to clarify the conditions under which digital tutors can meaningfully augment human-led instruction in higher education.
Findings The paper shows that the development of AI in education represents a cumulative progression in adaptivity, empathy, scalability and multimodal capabilities. Classical ITS improved learning outcomes when aligned with curriculum and assessment; affective and empathic systems expanded support to motivational and emotional processes; and LLM-based tools introduced open-domain dialogue, personalised feedback and research assistance at scale. Evidence indicates positive effects on academic performance, learner confidence and productivity, although these benefits remain heavily dependent on instructional design, user literacy and institutional governance. Significant risks persist, including academic integrity challenges, hallucination, bias, privacy concerns, technostress and over-reliance.
Conclusions (limits, implications etc.) The paper concludes that AI systems are most effective when conceptualised as complementary digital tutors embedded within human-led learning ecologies. Their successful adoption requires robust policies, explicit guidance for students, transparent system design and sustained teaching staff development. Current evidence is constrained by methodological limitations — short-term studies, small samples and reliance on self-reported perceptions — indicating the need for longitudinal, experimental and multi-stakeholder research to evaluate long-term educational impact and ensure responsible integration.

data.abstract: This experience report presents qualitative findings from a quasi-experimental study at Towson University examining ChatGPT's role as an evaluative partner in a junior-level business communication course. Across 15 course sections taught by five instructors, the intervention embedded AI feedback into the drafting process using rubric-based heuristics, staged integration, and reflective prompts. Post-semester faculty interviews revealed that when scaffolded intentionally, AI feedback reinforced instructor guidance, functioned as a “second reader,” and supported deeper revision, rhetorical awareness, and metacognitive growth—particularly among engaged students. However, instructors also reported uneven engagement, limited feedback literacy, and instances of misuse when students treated AI as a generative shortcut rather than a revision partner. These findings underscore the need for pedagogical guardrails, early integration, and explicit instruction in evaluative prompting. The study positions AI not as a replacement for human feedback but as part of a multi-voiced feedback ecosystem, blending machine and human perspectives to foster clarity, audience awareness, and confidence in student writing.

data.abstract: As technology reshapes language education, Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) offers new pathways for fostering learner autonomy and enhancing English proficiency. This study investigated the impact of CALL tools on English as an Additional Language (EAL) learners' autonomy in China, exploring how these tools support both independent vocabulary acquisition and classroom engagement. A sample of 100 undergraduate students participated in an 8-week intervention, with the experimental group using CALL tools (Anki, Quizlet, Kahoot!, and ChatGPT) and the control group following traditional textbook-based instruction. Data were collected through pre- and post-tests, digital analytics, and interviews. Quantitative results revealed significantly higher autonomy scores in the CALL group compared to the control group, supported by a moderate effect size. Qualitative analyses using NVivo indicated increased motivation, metacognitive awareness, and a preference for self-directed learning. Despite technical and usability barriers, most participants viewed CALL positively and expressed intentions to continue using these tools. The findings suggest that CALL-based activities significantly enhance students' autonomy, with the experimental group demonstrating greater improvement. The study concludes that CALL is an effective approach for fostering English language learning, and recommends integrating it into EAL classroom within a structured, guided framework to optimize learning outcomes.

Personalized rationale is an explanation of why a metacognitive strategy is relevant to a learner’s current writing. This study compared a personalized GenAI coaching package with template-based adaptive metacognitive prompting (AMP) in a nine-week randomized study of Chinese EFL undergraduates.
 
 
 
 Ninety-two participants completed pretest, posttest, and three-week delayed posttest assessments. Both conditions used the same Doubao LLM, interface, and trigger infrastructure. The AMP-Agent condition combined an essay-specific observation, personalized rationale, and an open-ended question; the AMP condition used template prompts.
 
 
 
 
 Analyses of questionnaire item responses found Group × Time interactions for self-regulated learning (SRL;
 p
 = 0.019) and GenAI dependency (
 p
 = 0.010), which also survived a retrospective Holm sensitivity correction across the three total outcomes. The SRL total contrasts at posttest and delayed posttest did not survive Bonferroni correction across time points. Self-reported GenAI dependency questionnaire scores were lower in the AMP-Agent group at both later assessments after this correction. Evidence for different writing-score trajectories was insufficient (interaction

 = 0.101). None of five highlighted behavioral transitions survived correction across 20 transition comparisons.
 
 
 
 
 The findings support a difference in self-reported regulation and dependency trajectories between the two prompting packages, while leaving the contribution of rationale alone, sustained writing benefits, and psychological mechanisms unresolved.

data.abstract: Penetration testing has long resisted full automation because it requires contextual reasoning, adaptive tool use, and experience-driven decision making across the Penetration Testing Execution Standard (PTES) lifecycle. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs), agentic reasoning, and multi-tool invocation have shifted the field from rule-based scripts and attack-graph reinforcement-learning planners toward interactive agents capable of planning, reflection, and environment interaction. The accompanying literature, however, suffers from inconsistent evaluation protocols, opaque scaffolding, and indiscriminate mixing of peer-reviewed papers with vendor self-reports, rendering headline claims difficult to compare. This work presents a critical narrative review with structured evidence charting of AI-assisted automated penetration testing between January 2023 and May 2026, retaining DeepExploit and AutoPentest-DRL as historical anchors. We introduce a dual-axis framework that annotates every finding by environment realism (R1–R4, from single-challenge CTFs to live enterprise networks) and source authority (A–D, from peer review to vendor self-report). Frontier agents reach 22–44% on R1 single-challenge CTFs (D-CIPHER), 79.17% on R2 AutoPenBench subtasks with a domain-tuned 32B model (xOffense), and 71.4% on the AISI 95-task expert tier (GPT-5.5), yet only 20–30% end-to-end completion on the R3 32-step TLO cyber range. On R4 live enterprise networks, the ARTEMIS multi-agent framework placed second overall against ten human professionals on an 8,000-host university network, submitting nine valid vulnerabilities at an 82% acceptance rate. Robust autonomy remains weak in long-horizon exploitation, Active Directory lateral movement, and defender-present environments. We argue that automated penetration testing is best framed as a systems-engineering problem rather than a single-model race, and we distinguish engineering-tractable Type A capability gaps from planning-bottlenecked Type B failures that require base-model reasoning improvements or reinforcement-learning post-training.

data.abstract: This study investigated the effectiveness of employing artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT and Grammarly, in developing the academic writing skills of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students at Israa University. A mixed-methods design was adopted, combining a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design with a focus group interview. The sample consisted of 20 students from the Department of English who participated in a five-week training program focusing on five-paragraph writing and the use of ChatGPT and Grammarly to review and improve their writing, with emphasis on six aspects of essay construction. Quantitative data were collected by analyzing students’ writing in the pretest and posttest, while qualitative data were obtained through the focus group interview. The findings revealed improvement in students’ posttest performance, particularly in idea organization, developing paragraphs, achieving textual coherence and cohesion, improving grammatical accuracy, and applying writing conventions. The interviews indicated that the tools provided immediate feedback during revision and editing, although some students expressed concerns about overreliance. Students also experienced difficulties in formulating topic sentences and selecting vocabulary, alongside cognitive, technical, linguistic, ethical, and affective challenges. The study recommends integration of AI tools into academic writing instruction, with strengthened teacher guidance to promote learner autonomy and maintain academic integrity.

data.abstract: This essay explores the intersection of medieval Christian mysticism and AI-generated imagery, reflecting on a six-week online course taught in summer 2024 at Drew University. A student’s experiments with AI-generated images of texts by Pseudo-Dionysius, Bernard of Clairvaux, Jan Ruusbroec, and Catherine of Genoa prompted reflection on pedagogy, ethics, and the representation of spiritual experience. Engaging ChatGPT as a dialogic partner, the author interrogates the capacities and limitations of AI to render mystical texts, considering issues of bias, historical context, creativity, and energy consumption. Using frameworks of purgation, illumination, and union, the essay examines how AI images mirror social and algorithmic constraints while offering opportunities for wonder, ethical reflection, and transformative learning. The discussion foregrounds questions of student-teacher dynamics, the construction of esprit de corps in online classrooms, and the role of generative AI in visualizing the ineffable. Readers are invited to participate in this exploratory, practice-oriented engagement with spirit.

data.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly transforming higher education by reshaping cognitive processes, learning behaviors, assessment practices and instructional approaches. This study examines the impact of AI on student learning through a combination of multi-institutional evidence and a quasi-experimental assessment in an undergraduate writing course. Three central dimensions are analyzed: cognitive offloading, critical versus naïve adoption of AI, and emerging learning patterns including normalization, confirmation bias and the erosion of scaffolding. Findings reveal that AI tools can enhance grammar accuracy, research efficiency, and factual recall, while also posing risks to creativity, critical thinking, independent revision and metacognitive engagement. The study highlights the importance of structured, critically mediated integration of AI into curricula to maximize learning benefits, uphold academic integrity and support long-term skill development

journal.name: Pacific Journal of Technology Enhanced Learning

data.abstract:
Operator Training Simulators (OTS) are commonplace in the chemical engineering industry but often underutilized in universities (Patle et al., 2019). Like a ‘flight simulator’ for engineers, they are ‘digital twins’ of real plants, that can run many safety scenarios. In tertiary education OTS offer scalable, active learning environments and authentic assessment, particularly when integrated with Generative AI (GenAI). Our pedagogical design is scaffolded through UTAUT2 (Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology), offering immersive, industry-aligned, practice-based engineering educational design (Honig et al., 2025), something that is often difficult to do in conventional classroom teaching (Honig et al., 2024). 
Within the ASE core themes, this presentation on OTS integration will focus on technology-enhanced learning and authentic assessment. It will draw on learnings from the integration of GenAI into the OTS software: while most people think of interacting with GenAI through text-interfaces (like ChatGPT) here students can interact through the game-interface itself (for example opening a valve or if an alarm trips, the GPT ‘knows’ and can automatically respond). 
  
In response to remote learning challenges presented during COVID-19 lockdowns (Honig et al., 2022), a modified industry-grade OTS (TSC Simulation) was embedded into undergraduate subjects. The simulator, originally designed for professional operator training, was adapted to educational needs by including assessment-focused scenarios and then augmented with a GPT-powered AI teaching assistant. Over four years, it has been used in both second- and third-year core Chemical Engineering subjects, providing students with a unique opportunity to interact with digital twins, analyze process safety incidents, and apply critical thinking in real-time problem-solving. 
  
Using a Design-Based Research framework, the initiative evolved through iterative cycles of student use, feedback, and redesign. Mixed methods evaluation involved pre- and post-use surveys grounded in the UTAUT framework, performance data from quizzes and assignments, and qualitative student feedback. The integration of GenAI was evaluated for usability, performance expectancy, and impact on learning outcomes. Students’ comprehension of safety concepts was compared across user groups—with and without chatbot access—using assessments and reflective discussions. 
  
Across cohorts, the OTS was rated highly for its realism and performance benefits, with a Likert average of 4.32 (out of 5) on performance expectancy. The GenAI chatbot, acting as a plant supervisor, facilitated guided root-cause analyses and reflection. Within a limited sample size, students with access to the AI assistant indicated higher quiz performance (67%) than those without (59%). However, effort expectancy for the OTS rated lower, highlighting the complexity of adapting industry-grade software to educational contexts. Improvements were made by redesigning activities to fall within students’ Zones of Proximal Development, particularly when supported with new GPT-based adaptive learning assistants, utilizing an agent structure. 
  
This initiative offers a replicable model for incorporating industry technologies and GenAI into curriculum-aligned, scalable assessment formats. It demonstrates how immersive learning tools can address gaps in traditional practicals, support student autonomy, and align with ASE’s call for flexible, digitally enhanced, and inclusive educational experiences. We will share initial learnings. 
Significant broader outcomes have also emerged from the work: as well integrating GPTs into simulators as AI-assistants for education, GPTs can similarly be integrated into real plants as AI-engineers for process control. 
  
The presentation will outline opportunities for GenAI integration into tertiary education, with a specific focus on integration into simulation based learning itself (as opposed to interaction through a chat interface). 
The presentation will have an interactive component allowing participants to build a customized chatbot through a purpose built interface for the conference presentation. 
  
References 
  
Honig, C., Rios, S., & Desu, A. (2025). Generative AI in engineering education: understanding acceptance and use of new GPT teaching tools within a UTAUT framework. Australasian Journal of Engineering Education, 1-13. 
Honig, C. D., Desu, A., & Franklin, J. (2024). GenAI in the classroom: Customized GPT roleplay for process safety education. Education for Chemical Engineers, 49, 55-66. 
Honig, C. D., Sutton, C. C., & Bacal, D. M. (2022). Off-campus but hands-on: Mail out practicals with synchronous online activities during COVID-19. Education for Chemical Engineers, 39, 84-93. 
Patle, D. S., Manca, D., Nazir, S., & Sharma, S. (2019). Operator training simulators in virtual reality environment for process operators: a review. Virtual Reality, 23, 293-311.

data.abstract: Simulation-based learning has established itself as a powerful instructional method in higher education, especially in domains that require complex interpersonal competencies such as counseling. Debriefing plays a pivotal role in transforming simulation experiences into meaningful learning by fostering critical reflection and integration of knowledge. While expert-facilitated debriefings are considered the gold standard, recent advancements in generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) have made chatbot-guided self-debriefings a scalable alternative. This study examines the effectiveness of moderated versus chatbot-supported debriefing formats following a Virtual Reality (VR)-based counseling simulation. A total of 45 undergraduate students in educational science participated in a controlled experiment. All participants engaged in a VR counseling scenario and were subsequently assigned to either a human-moderated or a chatbot-guided debriefing condition. The study investigated changes in counseling competence, self-efficacy, and learner perceptions across the two debriefing formats. Both self-efficacy and counseling competence increased significantly over time. The largest gains, particularly in counseling competence, were recorded after the debriefing, even though these gains were independent of the specific debriefing method employed. These findings underscore the importance of debriefing in educational contexts and indicate that a chatbot-based format could serve as a feasible alternative to traditional, moderator-led debriefings.

data.abstract: Krisna.ai is a web-based tool embedded in Sketchbook. This study describes the design, development, and evaluation of Krisna.ai. The system contains two main modules an Automatic Dialogue Function, based on a decision-tree approach to provide context-sensitive teaching replies, and an Automatic Questionnaire Function that allows structured reflection and formative assessment. Krisna.ai uses the DeepSeek API to enable interactive discussions between students and academics. It doesn’t compromise privacy since the AI is different from the one used by the faculty. Two experiments were done with 26 college students. The first evaluation studied the fluency, clarity and pedagogical worth of solution proposed by AI to open-ended academic questions. The second study evaluated engagement, understanding, and user choice between a chatbot-supported learning help and a static, manual question. Krisna.ai understands learner intention accurately, enhances user engagement, and allows learners to study in a systematic manner. Krisna.ai can help with the AI-empowered adaptive learning platform for education.

data.title: Resurrecting Socrates in the Age of AI: A Study Protocol for Evaluating a Socratic Tutor to Support Research Question Development in Higher Education

data.abstract: Formulating research questions is a foundational yet challenging academic skill, one that generative AI systems often oversimplify by offering instant answers at the expense of student reflection. This protocol lays out a study grounded in constructivist learning theory to evaluate a novel AI-based Socratic Tutor, designed to foster cognitive engagement and scaffold research question development in higher education. Anchored in dialogic pedagogy, the tutor engages students through iterative, reflective questioning, aiming to promote System 2 thinking and counteract overreliance on AI-generated outputs. In a quasi-experimental design, approximately 80 German pre-service biology teacher students will be randomly assigned to one of two groups: an AI Socratic Tutor condition and an uninstructed chatbot control. Across multiple cycles, students are expected to formulate research questions based on background texts, with quality assessed through double-blind expert review. The study also examines transfer of skills to novel phenomena and captures student perceptions through mixed-methods analysis, including surveys, interviews and reflective journals. This study aims to advance the understanding of how generative AI can be pedagogically aligned to support, not replace, human cognition and offers design principles for human-AI collaboration in education.

data.abstract: This study evaluated the impact of generative artificial intelligence tutoring on university students’ learning of differential calculus. A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design with a retention measure was conducted at the Universidad Técnica Estatal de Quevedo (Ecuador) with 160 first-semester students nested in eight intact class sections (80 in the AI condition and 80 in the control condition), selected through non-probabilistic convenience sampling. The ten-week intervention combined graduated hints, independent solution attempts, and critical verification of AI responses. The primary outcome was total achievement (0-100), with conceptual understanding, procedural fluency, self-regulated learning, and cognitive load as secondary outcomes. Models adjusted for pretest and prior achievement estimated a 6.10-point advantage for the AI condition at posttest (95% CI [4.50, 7.70], p < .001, partial η² = .264) and 7.39 points at retention (95% CI [5.57, 9.21], p < .001). The standardized effect was larger for conceptual understanding (g = 0.86) than for procedural fluency (g = 0.43). Within the AI condition, fidelity to the verification protocol was positively associated with achievement (β = .18, p = .001), whereas uncritical copying was negatively associated (β = -.13, p = .026). Findings indicate that the benefit of AI tutoring depends on the quality of the pedagogical interaction rather than on mere access to the tool

data.abstract: Self-regulated learning (SRL) is an approach to learning which aims to improve learners' learning outcomes. In the SRL cycle, the quality of students' reflections is a critical factor in SRL performance that can improve learning outcomes. The feedback provided by teachers often has a significant impact on the quality of students' reflections. However, research has shown that teachers are often confronted with many students and so are unable to give individual feedback. To address this problem, this study proposed chatbot-assisted SRL, which provides personal and immediate feedback during the SRL process to promote the quality of students' reflection. This study applied this approach in the "Website Design" unit of an Introduction to Multimedia course. Two classes of second-year university students were the participants. One class with 23 students was the experimental group using the chatbot-assisted SRL mode, whereas the other class with 24 students was the control group using the conventional SRL mode. The experiment results showed that the proposed approach improved the students' performance, motivation, SRL, reflection, and meta-cognition tendency more than the conventional SRL approach.

data.title: Shortcuts and scholarship: A cross-generational reflection on AI and academic formation

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1177/01634437261472373?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1177/01634437261472373, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Generative AI is changing not just how academic work gets done, but whether the processes that build genuine understanding are happening at all. This essay, written collaboratively by an early career researcher and a senior scholar in communication and media studies, argues that the real risk is not that AI will replace researchers, but that it will quietly erode the conditions under which researchers are formed, and indeed, what counts as research process. When doctoral students can produce coherent, polished outputs without sustained reading, critical thinking, or sitting with difficulty and uncertainty, something important is lost: the slow, often uncomfortable process through which understanding develops. Drawing on communication theory, critical pedagogy, and political economy, we examine the distinction between AI as a thinking tool and AI as a substitute for thought. We also argue that meaningful change requires institutional reform, not just better pedagogy. The machines are doing exactly what they are designed to do. The question is what we are designing our universities to do.

data.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has become an emerging educational tool with the potential to support critical thinking in students through explanation generation, immediate feedback, information analysis, argument comparison, and personalized learning support. This study aimed to analyze the contribution of generative artificial intelligence to strengthening critical thinking in higher education students, according to the scientific literature published between 2020 and 2026. according to the scientific literature published between 2020 and 2026. An integrative literature review was conducted using a systematic search process based on the identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion stages established by PRISMA 2020. The final corpus consisted of 15 publications related to generative artificial intelligence, ChatGPT, large language models, education, ethical use, student reasoning, and critical thinking. The findings were organized into four thematic categories: generative artificial intelligence and the development of critical thinking; feedback, personalization, and support for reasoning; ethics, technological dependence, and responsible use of AI; and teacher mediation, assessment, and educational limitations. The results indicate that generative AI can support critical thinking when it is used to question, compare, verify, and improve information rather than merely obtain automatic answers. However, its effectiveness depends on pedagogical design, teacher guidance, student responsibility, academic integrity, and the critical evaluation of AI-generated responses. It is concluded that generative artificial intelligence can strengthen critical thinking in students when implemented as a planned, ethical, and supervised educational strategy.

data.abstract: This study developed an AID (AI+Digital) Competency Enhancement Education Model by analyzing six generative AI-integrated courses at S University in 2025. Using Yin's multiple case study design, six courses across five disciplinary tracks were analyzed along four axes: teaching-learning, assessment, AI utilization, and competency design, drawing on course documents, student outputs, reflective journals, and surveys. Three AI utilization patterns were tentatively observed in these cases (Visualization, Hybrid Creative, and Simulation), alongside three shared patterns of change in teaching and learning: learners as active inquirers, critical verification as the core activity, and instructors as learning designers. The resulting AID Model integrates four design axes in a cyclical Explore→Generate→Verify→Reflect structure, with Human-in-the-Loop verification as a mandatory stage, a triple assessment structure (process, outcome, reflection), and five cumulatively developed competencies. Developed by iteratively comparing a theory-based analytic framework with real classroom data, the model addresses gaps in prior research including neglect of disciplinary specificity, optional treatment of verification, lack of integrated frameworks, and weak empirical grounding.

data.abstract: The rapid spread of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education presents significant opportunities for fostering engineering creativity. However, mere access is insufficient; structured AI literacy is essential. Drawing on the Human-AI Collaboration in Engineering Design (HAC-ED) framework, this study implemented a three-tier AI literacy training programme-covering tool comprehension, prompt optimization, and metacognitive regulation. In a quasi-experimental design, 70 undergraduate students in electronic information engineering first completed a baseline task without AI support, followed by an AI-assisted task. Participants were randomly assigned to an experimental group $(\mathrm{n}=35)$ with AI literacy training and DeepSeek-V3 use, or a control group $(\mathrm{n}=35)$ with the same model but no training. Creativity was assessed by independent experts on novelty, feasibility and scalability. Interaction quality (prompt accuracy and critical engagement) and psychological outcomes (self-efficacy and cognitive load) were captured from system logs and validated scales. Compared with the control group, the experimental group yielded solutions with significantly higher novelty $(\mathbf{t}(\mathbf{6 8})=\mathbf{2. 3 7}, \mathbf{p}=\mathbf{0. 0 2 0}, \mathbf{d}=\mathbf{0. 5 7})$ and scalability $(\mathbf{t}(\mathbf{6 8})=\mathbf{4. 1 1}, \mathbf{p}<\mathbf{0. 0 0 1}, \mathbf{d}=\mathbf{1. 0 0})$ with unchanged feasibility, crafted significantly more accurate prompts $(\mathbf{t}(\mathbf{6 8})=\mathbf{5. 1 6}, \mathbf{p}<\mathbf{0. 0 0 1}, \mathbf{d}=\mathbf{1. 2 6})$, demonstrated stronger critical interaction, reported significantly higher self-efficacy $(\mathrm{t}(68)=4.96$, $\mathrm{p}<0.001, \mathrm{d}=1.21)$ and lower cognitive load $(\mathrm{t}(68)=-4.30, \mathrm{p}<0.001$, $\mathrm{d}=-1.04)$. These findings advance understanding of how AI literacy training enhances engineering creativity and provide actionable implications for integrating GenAI into university engineering design education.

data.abstract: The rapid development of emerging technologies, such as generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), has led to a profound transformation in societal demands for talent. In addition to the increasing emphasis on technical training, core competencies, such as problem-solving, are recognized as crucial for the cultivation of high-quality talent. At present, learning environments supported by new technologies are widely used to promote educational reform, with particular focus on the impact of intelligent environments on metacognitive processes. However, research indicates that environments driven by a single technology often suffer from limitations, such as a lack of interactivity and insufficient generativity, which are significant but short-lived. This study focuses on an intelligent learning environment built upon the fusion of “GenAI+Metaverse” as the core variable, exploring its effect on the metacognitive abilities of college students. Using a four-dimensional metacognitive frameworkcomprising “awareness, planning, cognitive strategy, and monitoring”-this study compares the effects of traditional teaching, GenAI-supported teaching, and “GenAI + Metaverse” integrated teaching on students' metacognitive development. The results show that the integrated intelligent environment leads to positive changes across all metacognitive dimensions, with particularly significant improvements in task understanding and strategy execution. Furthermore, metacognitive ability is found to depend on the coordinated support of the technological environment, structured instructional design, strategic guidance, and reflection mechanisms. The study deepens the understanding of the interaction between intelligent technologies and metacognition, providing empirical evidence for the optimization of intelligent teaching environments in higher education and for the cultivation of interdisciplinary talent.

data.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Learning on Academic Performance and Critical Thinking Skills Among Undergraduate Students

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.70670/sra.v4i2.2401?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.70670/sra.v4i2.2401, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technologies in higher education, offering innovative opportunities to enhance personalized learning, academic achievement, and higher-order cognitive development. AI-powered educational tools, including intelligent tutoring systems, large language models, adaptive learning platforms, and automated feedback systems, are increasingly being integrated into undergraduate education to support teaching and learning processes. Despite their growing adoption, uncertainty remains regarding the extent to which structured AI-assisted learning may influence academic performance and critical thinking skills under optimized educational conditions. The present study employed a predictive research approach to evaluate the expected impact of varying levels of AI-assisted learning on academic performance, learning engagement, digital literacy, self-regulated learning, and critical thinking skills among undergraduate students. No surveys, interviews, classroom interventions, or assessments involving human participants were conducted. Instead, evidence-informed predictions were developed by integrating established scientific knowledge from educational psychology, artificial intelligence in education, cognitive science, personalized learning theory, self-regulated learning, and higher education research. Four educational conditions were comparatively evaluated: conventional learning without AI assistance (T₀), limited AI-assisted learning (T₁), moderate AI-assisted learning (T₂), and structured AI-assisted learning with instructor guidance (T₃). The predictive assessment suggests progressive improvements in academic achievement, learning efficiency, knowledge retention, research competency, digital literacy, and critical thinking with increasing integration of AI-supported learning under appropriate pedagogical supervision. Structured AI-assisted learning is predicted to provide the greatest educational benefits by combining personalized feedback, adaptive learning, instructor facilitation, and reflective evaluation while minimizing excessive dependence on artificial intelligence. The findings indicate that responsible integration of AI technologies has substantial potential to improve undergraduate education while preserving independent reasoning, analytical thinking, and evidence-based decision-making. The predictive framework developed in this study provides a scientific foundation for future experimental validation and responsible implementation of AI-assisted learning within higher education.

data.abstract:

humans and have a wide range of possible uses. Chatbots have showed potential in the field of medical education and health sciences by aiding learning, offering feedback, and increasing metacognitive thinking among undergraduate and postgraduate students. Chatbots are being used in the medical related field for teaching & learning, mental state categorisation, medication recommendation, health education and awareness. While chatbots have been well accepted by users, further study is needed to fully grasp their use in medical and healthcare settings.

This study looked at 32 research on ChatGPT and chatbots in medical-related fields and medical education. The findings show the exponential growth and potential of ChatGPT and chatbots in healthcare and medical education, as well as the necessity for more research and development in this sector.

data.title: College students' metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13619835, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Introduction Generative AI is increasingly used by college students for explanation, evaluation, and decision support, raising the question of whether perceived reliance accurately tracks the extent to which AI advice shapes final judgments. Methods In a three-condition between-subjects experiment, 342 undergraduate students completed reasoning and information-evaluation tasks under independent decision-making, open multi-turn ChatGPT support, or the same ChatGPT support with a brief metacognitive reflection prompt. Participants reported initial and final answers and confidence, and AI-assisted chat logs were coded for the final recommendation, its correctness, and behavioral reliance. Results Open ChatGPT support increased final confidence and was associated with 62.4% acceptance of incorrect AI advice. Reflection reduced incorrect-advice acceptance to 39.7% (OR = 0.40, 95% CI [0.28, 0.56], p < 0.001), improved awareness calibration (0.59 vs. 0.41, p < 0.001), and reduced the attribution-bias index (0.21 vs. 0.42, p = 0.002). Recommendation accuracy was comparable between the two AI-assisted groups. Discussion Brief metacognitive reflection improved immediate discrimination between useful and misleading AI advice without producing blanket rejection of AI. The exploratory association between calibration and overreliance is not interpreted as causal mediation, and the findings concern bounded academic decision tasks rather than long-term learning.

data.title: Multinational machine learning investigation of whether generative AI interactions augment or substitute cognitive skills and study efficiency in global higher education

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1007/s44163-026-02082-6?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-026-02082-6, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: While GenAI has been rapidly integrated into higher education, little empirical evidence explains how specific usage patterns drive cognitive augmentation versus cognitive offloading remains limited, as most studies treat usage uniformly. This study fills that gap by examining how GenAI habits, metacognitive behaviour, and emotions jointly predict cognitive skills and study efficiency as a distinct outcome across a global context. A secondary analysis was conducted on a publicly available cross-sectional multinational survey dataset of N = 14,949 higher education students, drawn from an original sample of 22,963 respondents across 120 countries. A five-layer analytical framework was applied: (1) measurement model validation using Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) and Fornell-Larcker criterion; (2) multivariate OLS regression was used to predict critical thinking gain; (3) benchmarking of four machine learning algorithm (Linear Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost and Gradient Boosting) was used on a stratified 70/30 train-test spilt; (4) SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was used on best performing model; and (5) K-Mean clustering (k = 4) was used across the three dimensions space of Cognitive Skill, Study Efficiency, and GenAI Usage. Robustness was assessed through five-fold cross-validation, discipline-stratified and subgroup analysis. The best-performing machine learning models demonstrated moderate predictive performance, explaining 28.18% of the variance in Cognitive Skill and 30.00% of the variance in Study Efficiency. The SHAP analysis result shows that Self-testing Habits (SHAP = 0.128) was the single strongest predictor of cognitive skill development. GenAI Usage Frequency (SHAP = 0.184) was the dominant driver of Study Efficiency. Four empirically distinct students’ interaction profiles were identified: (1) Augmentor (high skill, high efficiency, highest GenAI use; n = 2900); (2) Optimiser (moderate balance; n = 5500); (3) Traditionalist (efficient with lower GenAI use; n = 3000); and Substitutor (disengaged, low performance; n = 2000). Institutional funding type was a significant predictor of gains in study efficiency. The study concluded that effective human-GenAI interaction is not a function of usage frequency alone but of interaction quality, task type, and metacognitive structure within which AI tools are embedded. The cognitive skill efficiency trade-off is real but avoidable: Augmentor-profile students demonstrate that high efficiency and high cognitive skill co-exist when GenAI use is intensive, structured, and metacognitively scaffolded. Higher education institutions must move beyond binary use/no-use policies toward evidence-based frameworks that promote generative, metacognitively embedded interaction to maximise cognitive augmentation and mitigate passive substitution.

data.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has raised concern about cognitive laziness, a tendency of students to offload thinking processes to AI tools without critical engagement (Risko & Gilbert, 2016; Gerlich, 2025). This quasi-experimental study examined the effect of a Transformative Learning-based instructional design on mitigating AI-induced cognitive laziness among pre-service biology teachers studying the Bioethics topic within the Biotechnology course. A one-group pretest-posttest design was applied to 30 students of the Biology Education Study Program, FKIP Universitas Pasundan, selected through purposive sampling. The intervention was implemented in four stages adapted from Mezirow's framework: disorienting dilemma, critical reflection, reflective discourse, and action planning, applied to bioethical case analysis so that students had to justify positions instead of relying uncritically on AI-generated answers. Data were collected using a Cognitive Laziness Scale and analyzed using a paired-sample t-test and N-gain calculation. Results showed a statistically significant decrease in cognitive laziness scores from pretest to posttest (p < 0.05), with an average N-gain in the moderate category. Students demonstrated improved habits of verifying AI output and constructing independent ethical arguments. These findings suggest that Transformative Learning is a viable pedagogical strategy to preserve critical thinking amid increasing AI use in biotechnology and bioethics instruction

data.title: ChatGPT Scaffolding in Supporting Metacognition for Limit Concepts in Guided Inquiry Mathematics Learning

data.abstract:
Aim/Purpose: This study aims to investigate how ChatGPT-mediated scaffolding supports students’ metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, and evaluating strategies) in understanding limit concepts in calculus within a guided-inquiry learning environment.

Background: Guided inquiry fosters conceptual understanding in calculus, yet students often struggle with metacognitive regulation. While AI tools like ChatGPT offer interactive scaffolding, their impact on students’ self-regulated learning and problem-solving strategies in abstract topics, such as limits (a fundamental concept in calculus), remains underexplored. This study addresses this gap by evaluating ChatGPT’s function as a metacognitive guide in mathematics learning.

Methodology: A convergent mixed-methods design was implemented with 75 students of mathematics education at Universitas Jambi over a period of four weeks. Participants engaged in guided inquiry activities on limits, using ChatGPT for problem-solving and reflection. Data was collected through pre- and post-metacognitive assessments, screen recordings of ChatGPT-student interactions, and reflective journals. Quantitative data were analyzed using paired t-tests, while qualitative data were thematically coded to identify patterns in metacognitive engagement.

Contribution: This study advances understanding of AI’s capacity to foster self-regulated learning and critical thinking in mathematics, providing a framework for integrating generative AI as a metacognitive partner in guided inquiry pedagogy.

Findings: Results indicate significant improvements in metacognitive skills, particularly in monitoring and evaluation strategies. Qualitative analysis revealed that ChatGPT’s iterative feedback encouraged students to critically analyze solutions, particularly in identifying boundary conditions in limit problems. However, 28% of students passively accepted AI-generated answers without deeper scrutiny, highlighting variability in engagement levels.

Recommendations for Practitioners: Educators should integrate ChatGPT as a reflective tool in guided inquiry, designing structured activities that require students to justify or challenge AI-generated outputs. Providing explicit training in critical questioning techniques can enhance AI’s pedagogical value.

Recommendation for Researchers: Future research should explore long-term retention of metacognitive skills developed through AI scaffolding and adaptive AI models for optimizing ChatGPT-student interactions in mathematics education.

Impact on Society: The implications of this research extend beyond the classroom, potentially reshaping mathematics education in higher education. This approach could democratize access to personalized mathematical support, reduce educational inequalities, and prepare students for an AI-augmented professional landscape. However, careful consideration must be given to ethical implementation and the preservation of authentic mathematical thinking skills.

Future Research: Further studies should examine (1) the sustainability of AI-enhanced metacognitive development, (2) cross-cultural differences in AI scaffolding effectiveness, and (3) improved AI-driven adaptive learning strategies for mathematics education.

data.abstract: The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence has brought a number of ethical and practical issues to higher education. Solid experimental evidence is yet inadequate to set the functional rules for the new technology.The objective of this study is to analyse the experience of undergraduate students’ interaction with ChatGPT and contribute to identifying the problems arising from the widespread use of artificial intelligence.Junior university students (N = 25) were assigned the task of working on their seminar essays with the aid of ChatGPT. Most students were novices with this tool (the study was conducted in the spring of 2023). Their essays were analysed qualitatively, according to the principles of the general inductive approach.The initial attitudes towards artificial intelligence were almost equally distributed from enthusiastic to indifferent and cautious, with one student refusing to interact with the chatbot on ideological grounds. After the first experience, most of the students declared themselves adopters of the new technology. We have found some evidence for enhancing critical thinking competence when using ChatGPT, as well as examples of unquestioned reliance on its outputs. The tendency to personification of the chatbot was apparent in the students' essays.The findings show how easily the students embrace artificial intelligence and suggest a failure of any attempts for its strict regulation. This, on the other hand, underlines the need for emphasis on personal and research‐oriented approaches in teaching and learning.

data.abstract: : Routine-biased technological change (RBTC) has profoundly restructured the skill premium structure of the labor market, drastically compressed the living space of routine jobs, and thus exposed the structural lag of the traditional college employment guidance system in implicit competency mapping. This paper aims to deconstruct the dual mechanism of large language models (LLMs) in the micro-level employment intervention process. By comparing with the traditional static tutoring model, the study points out that LLMs, relying on their unstructured feature extraction capability, have effectively broken through the job search information barriers of job seekers and realized the paradigm shift from "typesetting polishing" to "dynamic semantic mapping". However, in practical application scenarios, the underlying alignment mechanism and text generation logic of algorithms can easily strip job seekers of their real practical baselines, inducing the risks of "ability falsification" and Akerlof's adverse selection in the labor market. To this end, this paper proposes that a high-fidelity dynamic game confrontation mechanism must be introduced into the intelligent empowerment framework, and the negative backlash of text "overstepping reconstruction" should be blocked through cognitive load limit testing, so as to provide a theoretical framework for the development of intelligent employment assistance systems with anti-reverse dependence attributes.

data.title: Generative AI dependency and self-perceived clinical decision-making in nursing students: A three-wave longitudinal study of metacognitive awareness as a mediator.

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1016/j.nedt.2026.107347?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nedt.2026.107347, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Generative artificial intelligence tools are increasingly used in nursing education, but excessive reliance on externally generated reasoning may be associated with reduced cognitive engagement. Evidence remains limited on whether within-person changes in generative artificial intelligence dependency are prospectively associated with nursing students' metacognitive awareness and self-perceived clinical decision-making.


OBJECTIVES
To examine longitudinal within-person associations among generative artificial intelligence dependency, metacognitive awareness, and self-perceived clinical decision-making, and to test whether metacognitive awareness mediates these associations.


DESIGN
A three-wave prospective longitudinal panel study.


SETTINGS
Nursing schools at three medical universities in China.


PARTICIPANTS
A convenience sample of 687 undergraduate nursing students completed the baseline survey; 618 students completed the third wave, yielding a retention rate of 90.0%.


METHODS
Data were collected at the beginning, middle, and end of one academic semester. A random-intercept cross-lagged panel model was used to separate stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations. Missing data were handled using full-information maximum likelihood. Common method bias was examined using Harman's single-factor test and an unmeasured latent method construct.


RESULTS
At the within-person level, higher generative artificial intelligence dependency was prospectively associated with lower metacognitive awareness at the subsequent wave (β = -0.18 to -0.21, p < .001). Higher metacognitive awareness was prospectively associated with higher self-perceived clinical decision-making (β = 0.22 to 0.25, p < .001). The indirect pathway from dependency to self-perceived clinical decision-making through metacognitive awareness was significant (standardized indirect effect = -0.045, 95% bootstrap confidence interval [-0.074, -0.019]), whereas the direct pathway was not statistically significant.


CONCLUSIONS
Generative artificial intelligence dependency was prospectively associated with students' self-perceived clinical decision-making through metacognitive awareness. Because the study was observational and the outcome was self-reported, the findings indicate an educational risk pathway rather than demonstrated clinical harm. Nursing educators may benefit from pairing artificial intelligence use with metacognitive scaffolding, verification routines, and reflective assessment.

data.title: When does ChatGPT help or hinder? A scoping review of influencing factors in college EFL learners' affective and cognitive experiences

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13658153, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Existing reviews have established the overall direction of ChatGPT's effects on college English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners' affective and cognitive experiences but have not systematically addressed under what conditions these effects arise. This scoping review maps the influencing factors reported in 26 empirical studies examining ChatGPT and closely related LLM-based generative AI tools as shaping these experiences. A systematic search of Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC following PRISMA-ScR guidelines and the (Arksey and O'malley, 2005) framework yielded 829 records, with 26 studies meeting inclusion criteria after deduplication and two-stage screening. Influencing factors were extracted from each study and organized into learner-level, instructional-level, and technology-level categories based on the Cognitive-Affective Theory of Learning with Media. Ten types of influencing factors were identified. Evidence density varied markedly across the three levels, with learner-level factors supported by the largest body of research and technology-level factors by the smallest. Self-efficacy showed consistent mediating pathways across eight studies, while metacognitive awareness produced the most clearly documented conditional differentiation between strategic and surface-level ChatGPT use. Structured instructional integration was the factor with the most consistently positive effects across the three studies that examined it. The influencing factor mapping table reveals that the effects of ChatGPT on EFL learners are not uniform but contingent on the interaction among learner characteristics, instructional design, and technology use patterns, supporting differentiated rather than uniform approaches to ChatGPT integration in college EFL instruction.

data.abstract: ChatGPT is an artificial intelligence (AI)-based chatbot that has expanded in popularity among users in several fields. It could transform education and support achieving sustainable development goals. Providing counseling and mental health services is a vital national goal for maintaining sustainable goals. As evidence of innovative technology’s ability to support sustainability in the digital era, no study has been found to investigate ChatGPT in counseling and mental health education based on students’ perceptions and experiences. Consequently, this study aimed to explore undergraduates’ perceptions in terms of the benefits and challenges of using ChatGPT in counseling and mental health education. The study adopted a descriptive quantitative approach using a purposive sample comprising 210 respondents who enrolled in the counseling and mental health program at the University of Jordan and experienced ChatGPT in their learning. The results reported that 81.9 percent of respondents perceived ChatGPT as a beneficial learning tool for counseling and mental health (M = 4.10); they perceived their ability to support most of the primary counseling skills and therapeutic conditions as the counseling dispositions and behaviors expected for reflection on meaning skills, empathic care, setting boundaries with colleagues, openness to feedback, congruence and genuineness, ability to record-keeping and task completion, and non-verbal skills. Furthermore, the findings reported that students experienced moderate challenges and concerns while utilizing ChatGPT (M = 3.21). The study’s findings suggest educators in counseling and mental health employ ChatGPT in the teaching and learning process. In addition, it proposes that decision-makers at the University of Jordan consider student concerns about ChatGPT.

data.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping higher education, especially in technology-oriented programs where critical thinking and complex problem solving are core outcomes. This study triangulates global and local evidence on performance/efficiency, usage, autonomy, critical-thinking engagement, and ethics by combining a systematized review informed by Kitchenham and structured using selected PRISMA 2020 elements (2020–2025; last search: May 2025; 49 studies; Scopus, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, and SpringerLink; not prospectively registered) with an anonymous survey of 302 computing and engineering students from a single university in Ecuador. The expert-reviewed instrument showed acceptable internal consistency for most scale-based dimensions (McDonald’s ω), whereas institutional and ethics-related items were analyzed primarily at the item level. Results showed near-universal academic GenAI use (96%), with 47% of students reporting weekly use and 26% daily use. Research-related work was the most frequent application (81.5%), followed by homework (48.3%), report writing (43.7%), and exam preparation (41.7%). Although students reported perceived efficiency gains, concerns persisted about reduced analytical engagement and technological dependence (84.1%). Ethical concerns centered on dependence, authenticity, and data privacy, while institutional responses pointed to the need for formal training (96.7%) and clearer guidance. Based on this triangulation, we propose a context-bounded interpretive framework suggesting that GenAI’s educational value depends on instructional and governance conditions that preserve autonomy, critical thinking, integrity, and equity.

journal.name: 2026 IEEE International Conference on AI and Data Analytics (ICAD)

data.abstract: The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into higher education is enabling unprecedented scale in knowledge retrieval and synthesis. However, getting real value from it requires a shift in how people engage, moving from passively checking AI outputs to actively taking responsibility for what gets accepted. Synthetic Socratic Inquiry (SSI) is introduced in this paper as a framework for embedding ‘constructive challenge’ directly into the way people work with AI. Through the integration of Modular Prompting architectures with the R.E.D. (Recognize, Evaluate, Draw Conclusions) Model, the operational dynamics of GenAI are reconfigured from a statistical generation tool to those of a structured ‘sparring partner.’ Additionally, the Trust Calibration Index (TCI) is presented as a diagnostic tool for evaluating validation behaviors in learning exchanges. Preliminary results point to an ‘Efficiency Paradox’: the extra steps SSI requires do slow things down, but those steps also catch more errors and sharpen the quality of reasoning. Rather than restricting access to GenAI, SSI enforces a verifiable reasoning workflow that preserves critical thinking. A preliminary classroom study (n = 34) comparing structured SSI prompting against open-ended baselines reported a 38% reduction in citation errors and a more than fivefold increase in assumptionflagging (4.2 vs.0.8 events per session), providing early evidence that the framework shifts measurable verification behavior, not just dispositions.

data.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet evidence from Philippine computing programs remains limited. This study examined whether student characteristics and generative AI use patterns are associated with academic outcomes among Bachelor of Science in Information Technology (BSIT) undergraduates at a Philippine public university. Using a quantitative-dominant mixed-methods design, the study administered a descriptive–correlational survey to 60 randomly selected students and used short interviews and open-ended responses to contextualize the quantitative results. Descriptive statistics summarized participant characteristics and tool use, while multivariate tests examined associations with perceived academic benefits and self-reported academic performance. Most respondents reported frequent use and high familiarity and described benefits for engagement, idea development, and learning flexibility. However, students also reported distraction, overreliance, and occasional inaccuracies. Age, frequency of use, and familiarity were significantly associated with academic outcomes, whereas gender and year level were not. The findings indicate that generative AI can support student learning when institutions pair curricular integration with verification practices, ethical-use guidance, and assessment designs that preserve independent thinking.

data.abstract: Writing skills are essential in higher education as they enable students to communicate ideas clearly and succeed academically. However, many undergraduates struggle with clarity, coherence, and creativity in their writing. This study examined the effect of ChatGPT-based learning support on English essay writing among 341 first-year Bachelor of Education students at the University of Nairobi. Guided by social constructivist learning theory and Cognitive Load Theory, a quasi-experimental one-group pre-test/post-test design was used. Students completed standardized writing tests before and after a one-month period of ChatGPT-assisted learning integrated into classroom instruction. Data were collected through tests, questionnaires, and observations, then analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics. ANOVA results confirmed significant improvement, F(1,307) = 69.14, p < .001. Students who perceived ChatGPT as beneficial showed the largest improvements (19.87 to 25.21) compared to those with neutral perceptions (20.19 to 23.91) and those who did not consider it supportive (20.67 to 22.13). The strongest effects were linked to personalized feedback, grammar support, constant availability, and structured guidance. Observations and qualitative data indicated higher motivation, engagement, and self-correction. Despite concerns about factual reliability, students applied fact-checking and evaluation strategies. The study concludes that ChatGPT is an effective supplementary tool for improving ESL academic writing and recommends its integration within pedagogical frameworks that foster critical thinking and verification.

A helping hand or a dominant partner? Individual perceptions of
 GenAI
 reliance and human agency in collaborative learning

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1111/bjet.70090?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.70090, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become a routine source of feedback, explanation, drafting support and task guidance in higher education. This study examined how individual students' self‐reported GenAI reliance and perceived human agency co‐varied over time in an AI‐supported collaborative writing course. Three‐wave data were collected from 342 undergraduates working in 85 fixed groups. A traditional cross‐lagged panel model (CLPM) and a random intercept cross‐lagged panel model (RI‐CLPM) were estimated to distinguish observed‐level associations from within‐person temporal relations after stable between‐person differences were separated. The CLPM indicated reciprocal observed‐level associations. In the RI‐CLPM, higher‐than‐usual reliance was associated with lower subsequent agency, whereas agency‐to‐reliance paths were weaker and not statistically supported. Equality‐constraint tests were consistent with directional asymmetry, while 95% confidence intervals and Monte Carlo sensitivity analyses showed that small reverse effects remain possible. Backend logs showed that self‐reported reliance corresponded to AI‐use intensity, although log indicators could not distinguish strategic consultation from cognitive offloading or deference. The findings highlight the importance of designing AI‐supported collaboration so that students' responsibility for interpretation, judgement and authorship remains visible.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 GenAI systems can provide timely feedback, explanation and drafting support in collaborative learning environments.
 
 
 AI support may help students generate ideas and revise work, but reliance on system‐generated suggestions can reduce opportunities for judgement, negotiation and ownership.
 
 
 Traditional cross‐lagged models can conflate stable between‐person differences with within‐person temporal associations.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 The study examines individual students' self‐reported GenAI reliance and perceived human agency across three waves in an AI‐supported collaborative writing course.
 
 
 After stable between‐person differences were separated, RI‐CLPM estimates provided stronger evidence for paths from higher‐than‐usual reliance to lower subsequent agency than for the reverse direction.
 
 
 Equality‐constraint tests were consistent with directional pattern asymmetry, while confidence intervals and Monte Carlo sensitivity analyses indicated that small agency‐to‐reliance effects remain possible.
 
 
 Backend logs showed that self‐reported reliance corresponded to AI‐use intensity, but log indicators could not distinguish strategic consultation from cognitive offloading or deference.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 AI‐supported collaborative tasks should make students' responsibility for interpretation, judgement and authorship visible throughout the learning process.
 
 
 Instructors can ask groups to form an initial position before invoking AI and to explain why AI suggestions are accepted, revised or rejected.
 
 
 GenAI tools may better support agency by offering critics, asking questions and prompting reflection while leaving decisions about task direction to students.
 
 
 Learning analytics dashboards should not equate high AI‐use intensity with over‐reliance unless log data are interpreted alongside discourse, reflection, revision or decision‐making evidence.

data.title: Can theory-driven learning analytics dashboard enhance human-AI collaboration in writing learning? Insights from an empirical experiment

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19364, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: The integration of Generative AI (GenAI) into education has raised concerns about over-reliance and superficial learning, particularly in writing tasks in higher education. This study explores whether a theory-driven learning analytics dashboard (LAD) can enhance human-AI collaboration in the academic writing task by improving writing knowledge gains, fostering self-regulated learning (SRL) skills and building different human-AI dialogue characteristics. Grounded in Zimmerman's SRL framework, the LAD provided real-time feedback on learners'goal-setting, writing processes and reflection, while monitoring the quality of learner-AI interactions. A quasi-experiment was conducted involving 52 postgraduate students divided into an experimental group (EG) using the LAD to a control group (CG) without it in a human-AI collaborative writing task. Pre- and post- knowledge tests, questionnaires measuring SRL and cognitive load, and students'dialogue data with GenAI were collected and analyzed. Results showed that the EG achieved significantly higher writing knowledge gains and improved SRL skills, particularly in self-efficacy and cognitive strategies. However, the EG also reported increased test anxiety and cognitive load, possibly due to heightened metacognitive awareness. Epistemic Network Analysis revealed that the EG engaged in more reflective, evaluative interactions with GenAI, while the CG focused on more transactional and information-seeking exchanges. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on the educational use of GenAI and highlight the importance of designing interventions that complement GenAI tools, ensuring that technology enhances rather than undermines the learning process.
